title: A Special Focus on Men’s Health
note: Demo snapshot of public ifanca.org content, for a training session only. Not an official IFANCA dataset. Content may be out of date. Check ifanca.org for current information.

blocks.text: AS WOMEN FACE SPECIFIC HEALTH CHALLENGES due to their hormonal makeup and anatomy, men also face health challenges for the same reasons. Men’s health is tied to their unique reproductive system and lifestyle behaviors. We’ll start with health issues that originate in the male reproductive system.

Men are at risk for prostate cancer and testicular cancer. Prostate cancer is one of the most common forms of cancer. The prostate is a small, walnut-shaped gland that produces seminal fluid that transports and develops sperm. When prostate cancers develop, if they stay inside the prostate gland, they may not cause serious harm, and only need minimal treatment. However, some cancers grow aggressively and spread quickly. Common symptoms of prostate cancer include trouble urinating, blood in the urine, blood in the semen, erectile dysfunction, and unintentional weight loss. The cause of prostate cancer is unknown, but risk factors include a family history of prostate cancer and obesity. The risk of getting prostate cancer increases after age 50.

Testicular cancer isn’t very common and is highly treatable. The testicles make sperm and the hormone testosterone inside of the scrotum. Testicular cancer can occur at any age but mostly happens between the ages of 15 and 45. The first sign of cancer is usually a bump or lump on the testicle. Other signs can include back pain, discomfort in the testicle or scrotum, a dull ache in the lower belly or groin, and enlargement of breast tissue.

Men experience declining levels of testosterone as they age or due to certain health conditions. This is also referred to as low testosterone or male hypogonadism. Testosterone, the androgen produced in the testicles, is the key ingredient in male hormonal development as it can affect appearance, sex drive, muscle build, and bone mass. These symptoms of low testosterone can be emotionally and physically challenging. The symptoms include decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, fatigue, hair loss, decreased cognitive function, decreased sperm count, increased body fat, loss of muscle mass, and decreased bone density.
Similar diseases affect men and women differently. Cardiovascular diseases affect both men and women, but men tend to develop it at earlier ages.
“Heart disease is the leading cause of death for men, women, and people of most racial and ethnic groups.”

Men are also more likely to have heart attacks and a higher risk for coronary artery disease. According to an article on WedMD, “just being a man makes you more likely to get heart disease at a younger age — about 10 years earlier on average.” Low testosterone and erectile dysfunction could be signs of future heart problems.

Men tend to develop type 2 diabetes at a lower weight than women. Because men tend to accumulate fat around the abdomen, this trait is associated with higher risk for type 2 diabetes, rather than the pear-shaped fat distribution often common with women. Erectile dysfunction shows up as a common symptom along with an overactive bladder, incontinence, urinary tract infections, and retrograde ejaculation (when semen is released into the bladder). Undiagnosed or unmanaged diabetes can lead to other health problems such as stroke, vision loss, kidney failure, heart disease, or the amputation of a toe, foot, or leg. We can see how all these ailments are linked to one another.

Men are at a slightly higher risk for colon cancer than women with the lifetime risk of developing colorectal cancer being about one in 23 for men and one in 25 for women. Excluding skin cancers, colorectal cancers are the third most diagnosed cancers in the US. In an article for Men’s Health magazine, Marty Munson states, “Colorectal cancer is a big risk: It’s currently the third leading cause of both new cancers and cancer deaths for men (behind lung and prostate). And while colorectal cancer rates are declining for people ages 65 and older, they’re climbing for younger people—especially men.” The symptoms of colorectal cancers usually depend on the size of the cancer and where it is in the large intestine. The symptoms include blood in the stools or rectal bleeding, changes in bowel habits such as frequent diarrhea or constipation, fatigue, discomfort in the belly area, and losing weight without trying.

There are lifestyle choices that play a role in men’s health. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, “although men just make up over half of the workforce, they experience more than 90 percent of workplace fatalities.” Men are more likely to be in occupations that involve a higher risk of being injured or exposure to hazardous substances. These jobs usually involve construction or industrial work. If your father, brother, or uncle works in construction, transportation, or health care, he’s probably experienced at least one type of injury.

Also, according to the Indiana University School of Medicine “Men are significantly less likely than women to see a doctor or report symptoms to a health care provider. Only 60 percent of men go to the doctor for a yearly, routine checkup, and 40 percent won’t go until something is seriously wrong.” Often, men will avoid health issues, hoping they will resolve on their own. Or, if they do seek medical attention, they may not be completely forthcoming about all their problems. Part of this avoidance is rooted in fear. But it is also rooted in the negative feelings of vulnerability and the societal pressure men feel to be “superheroes” or to “man up.” Easily treatable illnesses can evolve into life threatening diseases due to fear and avoidance.
This avoidance also extends into maintaining their mental health. Men may not seek out counseling because of unhealthy societal expectations of masculinity.
“There is a social stigma for men, in seeking help, and the fear of appearing weak or fragile. The pressure to “man up” and appear unemotional has long-lasting, detrimental consequences.”

blocks.text: Some may choose to mask their emotional symptoms, like depression or anxiety, with unhealthy coping habits such as smoking, unhealthy eating, or substance abuse. Although women are more likely to attempt suicide, men are more likely to die by suicide, and often through violent means. The American Foundation for Suicide Prevention states, “in 2022, men died by suicide 3.85 times more than women.”

But there is light at the end of the tunnel. So many of these issues can be avoided with a healthy diet, moderate exercise, and preventive healthcare. Guidelines vary for when men should start their annual physicals, but from ages 18 to 39, they should be every two to three years. From ages 40 and above, exams should be done annually. These exams are to check for issues with blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood glucose. Prostate cancer screening usually starts at 50 but may start earlier if you are African American or have a family history of prostate cancer. Men can perform self-examinations to check for testicular cancer. This is recommended for those between the ages of 20 and 40 years old. Colon cancer screenings start at age 45. Mental health screenings can start at any time when feelings of ongoing sadness or anxiety are detected.

When concerning men’s health, it is important for men to put aside their fears and reservations. If you are in pain, whether that pain is physical, mental, emotional, or spiritual, please seek professional help. Don’t “tough it out.”
“Do not let toxic ideas of masculinity prevent you from living a happy, healthy life.”

Abdullah bin Amru bin Al-‘As narrated that Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) advised us, “Your body has a right on you,” (Sahih al-Bukhari 1975). Our minds and bodies have rights over us, and they must be valued as the precious gifts they are.
Kelly Izdihar Crosby is an artist and freelance writer living in Atlanta, GA.
